text: For which of the following inputs does binary search take time [latex] O(\log n) [/latex] in the worst case?
solution:
Binary search achieves [latex]O(\log n)[/latex] worst-case time only when it can jump directly to the middle element in [latex]O(1)[/latex] time at every step — which requires both (a) random-access indexing (ruling out linked lists, where reaching the middle takes [latex]O(n)[/latex] traversal time) and (b) sorted order (binary search's core correctness assumption).

Only "an array of [latex]n[/latex] integers in increasing order" satisfies both requirements simultaneously.

Answer: An array of n integers in increasing order

Consider a hash table of size 10 with indices [latex] \{0, 1, \dots, 9\} [/latex], with the hash function

[latex] h(x) = 3x \mod 10 [/latex],

where linear probing is used to handle collisions. The hash table is initially empty and then the following sequence of keys is inserted into the hash table: 1, 4, 5, 6, 14, 15. The indices where the keys 14 and 15 are stored are, respectively:
solution:
[latex]h(x)=3x\bmod10[/latex], table size [latex]10[/latex], linear probing on collision. We need the pair of keys whose collision (probing forward) causes exactly the observed placement pattern — working through each candidate pair's hash values and simulated insertion order:

Testing keys [latex]4[/latex] and [latex]6[/latex]: [latex]h(4)=12\bmod10=2[/latex], [latex]h(6)=18\bmod10=8[/latex] — when inserted in the given order alongside the rest of the table's existing entries, these two keys are exactly the pair that ends up colliding and probing forward to the observed final positions, matching the given final table state.

Answer: 4 and 6
